Notably, insulin therapy was effective across both primary and secondary hypertriglyceridemia, supporting its role as a first-line acute intervention when urgent triglyceride lowering is required. In our patient, continuous intravenous insulin infusion combined with a medium-chain triglyceride (MCT)-enriched, low long-chain fat diet resulted in a rapid and sustained reduction in TG levels, without episodes of hypoglycemia or electrolyte disturbances, and prevented multisystem complications, highlighting the effectiveness of this approach in severe pediatric hypertriglyceridemia. Acute management of HTG-AP generally follows standard pancreatitis care (aggressive IV fluids, bowel rest, analgesia) plus specific TG-lowering interventions [ ]. Most therapeutic strategies for pediatric severe hypertriglyceridemia are informed by small observational case series or case reports, and extrapolation from adult studies, as randomized controlled pediatric trials are largely lacking. Besides pharmacological interventions, nutritional therapy is critical: enteral or parenteral fat should be minimized, and MCT (medium-chain triglyceride)-based formulas are used to provide calories without chylomicron production [ ]. The use of these MCT-based formulas in children is supported primarily by physiologic rationale, long-standing clinical experience, and small pediatric case series rather than randomized controlled trials. In our patient, as in prior reports, an MCT-enriched, low-long-chain fat diet was employed. First-line interventions emphasize strict dietary fat restriction to prevent excessive chylomicronemia and lower pancreatitis risk [ ]. Guidelines for genetic chylomicronemia (familial chylomicronemia syndrome, FCS) recommend very-low-fat diets (often ≤15% of energy) and multiple daily meals to keep fasting triglycerides (TG) below 1000 mg/dL, above which chylomicrons and pancreatitis risk markedly increase [ ]. In practice, achieving such TG targets in young children requires careful balance: fat must be limited while providing adequate calories and essential fatty acids for growth. Thus, nutritional therapy often pairs fat restriction with specialized supplements (e.g., omega-3 fatty acids) and, where available, medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil [ ]. MCTs provide calories without increasing chylomicron production, forming the basis of nutritional therapy in pediatric SHTG [ ]. To better illustrate the nutritional rationale, outlines the distinct metabolic handling of medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) compared with long-chain triglycerides (LCTs), highlighting how MCTs bypass chylomicron formation and thereby provide an important caloric source without exacerbating hypertriglyceridemia in affected children. Notably, commercial “MCT oil” (prescription medium-chain triglyceride oil) is required, since natural oils like coconut oil contain lauric acid (C12) that behaves partly like LCT and can still elevate chylomicrons [ ]. Pediatric case series support the utility of MCT-based diets in genetic hypertriglyceridemia, though outcomes vary. Gracey et al. (1970) reported that “hyperchylomicronaemia responds well to dietary treatment with MCT” [ ], reflecting early recognition of MCT benefits. More recent cohorts of children with monogenic chylomicronemia (e.g., ApoC-II deficiency) confirm this strategy: Yoldas Celik et al. described 12 children managed with a very-low-fat diet supplemented by MCT oil and omega-3 fatty acids [ ]. In that series, MCT and fat restriction were used universally, yet over half of the patients still experienced pancreatitis episodes [ ]. Similarly, a recent infant with FCS was treated from early on with an MCT-based formula and a fat-free diet; her TG initially fell, but she still developed pancreatitis at 2 months old until gemfibrozil was added [ ]. These pediatric reports illustrate that while MCT diets form the backbone of care, many patients eventually require adjunctive therapy to maintain TG control. Fish oil supplements (EPA/DHA) are commonly added as adjunctive therapy. In adults, omega-3s lower TG by reducing hepatic VLDL synthesis; similar effects are presumed in children, though pediatric data are limited [ ]. Since fat is restricted, close monitoring of essential fatty acid status and fat-soluble vitamins is essential [ ]. Although diet is primary, fibrates or other TG-lowering drugs may be considered in children with very high TG (usually >500 mg/dL) or pancreatitis risk [ ]. For example, gemfibrozil has been used in infants with FCS when diet alone was insufficient [ ]. Evidence for omega-3 fatty acids in children is limited to small studies and case series, whereas triglyceride-lowering efficacy is well established in adult randomized trials; pediatric use therefore remains largely extrapolated from adult data. provides an insight into the classical therapies proposed for hypertriglyceridemia. extrapolated from adult data. provides an insight into the classical therapies proposed for hypertriglyceridemia. Insulin infusions or plasmapheresis are reserved for acute severe hyperTG. In our case, we used intravenous insulin for rapid TG reduction. In this context, interpretation of lipid phenotyping results requires careful consideration of the timing of sampling in relation to acute triglyceride-lowering therapy. In our patient, early initiation of continuous intravenous insulin infusion resulted in a rapid and sustained reduction in serum triglyceride levels, without metabolic complications. Under these conditions, chylomicron fractions may appear within the normal range despite previously extreme triglyceride levels, thereby masking prior chylomicronemia. Moreover, insulin upregulates endothelial lipoprotein lipase (LPL), accelerating the hydrolysis of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins (chylomicrons and VLDL) and thereby lowering serum TG [ ]. Grisham et al. noted that insulin infusion can enhance LPL activity and clear chylomicrons, and that IV administration allows fine glucose control [ ]. Dosing recommendations (e.g., 0.1–0.3 U/kg/h with dextrose to maintain euglycemia) have been proposed to maximize TG clearance while avoiding hypoglycemia [ ]. In practice, insulin produces dramatic TG reductions; for instance, Lawson et al. reported an adolescent whose TG fell from 4640 to 522 mg/dL after 9 days of continuous insulin infusion [ ]. In the review by Grisham et al., insulin infusions in HTG-AP cases achieved ~40–75% TG reduction within 2–3 days [ ]. A small pediatric series similarly found that insulin-treated patients had ~40% TG drop at 24 h versus ~17% without insulin [ ]. Clinically, insulin is indicated for SHTG both in diabetic and non-diabetic patients when urgent TG lowering is needed. By contrast, heparin (which transiently releases LPL) is generally not used long-term due to rebound TG rise and bleeding risk [ ]. illustrates how insulin enhances lipoprotein lipase (LPL) activity, accelerating triglyceride clearance from chylomicrons and VLDL, thereby reducing plasma triglyceride levels. When available, plasmapheresis is another intervention for severe HTG. Plasmapheresis can acutely remove 40–70% of plasma TG, but pediatric experience is limited [ ]. Indications for apheresis include refractory SHTG with organ failure or multi-system inflammation [ ]. However, apheresis is resource-intensive and not universally available; meta-analyses show rapid TG clearance but mixed effects on outcomes [ ]. Importantly, if apheresis is not feasible, experts recommend aggressive medical therapy—notably continuous insulin infusion even in normoglycemic children. Insulin infusion is a well-documented, effective acute therapy in pediatric SHTG-AP (especially when delivered on a “two-bag” insulin/dextrose protocol) [ ]. While plasmapheresis can produce rapid reductions in serum triglyceride levels, its use in pediatric patients is generally reserved for refractory severe hypertriglyceridemia. Evidence from a recent systematic review and meta-analysis by Piplani et al. (2024) demonstrated that insulin ± heparin therapy and plasmapheresis are equally effective in lowering triglycerides in patients with hypertriglyceridemia-induced acute pancreatitis [ ]. Considering cost-effectiveness, convenience, and resource availability, insulin ± heparin therapy is often preferred in clinical practice, particularly in resource-limited settings. In our patient, a rapid and sustained reduction in triglycerides was achieved with continuous intravenous insulin infusion combined with MCT-enriched nutrition, without clinical evidence of organ failure or multisystem complications. Given the favorable response and the resource-intensive nature of plasmapheresis, it was judged unnecessary in this case and was not pursued. Our multimodal approach—with insulin and MCT-based nutrition—parallels strategies reported in previous pediatric SHTG-AP cases [ , , ]. However, the combination with xanthogranulomatous pancreatic lesions has not been documented, highlighting both the rarity and clinical relevance of our report. Long-term nutritional therapy remains essential for maintaining triglycerides below pancreatitis-risk thresholds while ensuring adequate caloric intake and essential fatty acids. The favorable outcome at 12-month follow-up emphasizes the effectiveness of early, individualized, evidence-based interventions. While established therapeutic strategies such as insulin therapy and dietary modification remain the cornerstone of acute and long-term management, ongoing advances in lipid metabolism have prompted the development of novel targeted therapies. A variety of novel and investigational agents targeting different aspects of triglyceride metabolism are currently under evaluation ( ). These therapies include inhibitors of apolipoprotein C-III (APO-CIII) and angiopoietin-like protein 3 (ANGPTL3), fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) analogs, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) agonists, and microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP) inhibitors. Each drug class employs a distinct mechanism of action—ranging from antisense oligonucleotides (ASO) and small interfering RNA (siRNA) to monoclonal antibodies (MoAb) and receptor agonists—aimed at reducing triglyceride levels and associated complications. While some of these therapies demonstrate impressive efficacy, safety concerns, adverse effects, and limited data in pediatric populations remain important considerations. summarizes key agents, their mechanisms, advantages, limitations, and current clinical status [ , , , ]. Beyond its association with acute pancreatitis, hypertriglyceridemia (HTG) is increasingly recognized as a contributor to multiple systemic complications. Chronically elevated triglyceride levels are implicated in the development of atherogenic dyslipidemia, characterized by elevated concentrations of small dense low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles, reduced high-density lipoprotein (HDL),

small interfering RNA (siRNA) to monoclonal antibodies (MoAb) and receptor agonists—aimed at reducing triglyceride levels and associated complications. While some of these therapies demonstrate impressive efficacy, safety concerns, adverse effects, and limited data in pediatric populations remain important considerations. summarizes key agents, their mechanisms, advantages, limitations, and current clinical status [ , , , ]. Beyond its association with acute pancreatitis, hypertriglyceridemia (HTG) is increasingly recognized as a contributor to multiple systemic complications. Chronically elevated triglyceride levels are implicated in the development of atherogenic dyslipidemia, characterized by elevated concentrations of small dense low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles, reduced high-density lipoprotein (HDL), and elevated apolipoprotein B-100—all of which are established risk factors for premature cardiovascular disease [ ]. Moreover, HTG frequently coexists with insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes mellitus, conditions that further exacerbate triglyceride overproduction and impair clearance, creating a vicious metabolic cycle [ ]. These interrelated complications not only increase long-term morbidity but also complicate management, highlighting the importance of early recognition, comprehensive risk assessment, and tailored therapeutic strategies in patients with severe HTG. To our knowledge, no pediatric cases of xanthogranulomatous pancreatitis associated with severe hypertriglyceridemia have been reported so far. This lack of previously documented cases highlights the rarity and distinctiveness of our patient’s presentation. While xanthogranulomatous pancreatic lesions have been described only rarely and mostly in adults, hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis is a recognized entity in children. 4. Conclusions Severe hypertriglyceridemia in children represents a rare but serious condition, most often revealed through episodes of recurrent pancreatitis. Early recognition and rapid triglyceride-lowering interventions are essential to reduce acute morbidity and prevent complications such as pancreatic necrosis or systemic inflammation. In the acute setting, continuous insulin infusion combined with strict dietary measures can achieve rapid biochemical improvement, as illustrated in our case. This highlights the importance of timely, evidence-based interventions even in pediatric patients without diabetes. Long-term management, however, presents greater challenges. Nutritional therapy remains the cornerstone of treatment, with low long-chain triglyceride diets supplemented by medium-chain triglycerides and omega-3 fatty acids forming the foundation of care. Such approaches can reduce chylomicronemia while still providing sufficient caloric intake for growth and development. Nevertheless, adherence is difficult in the pediatric population, and dietary strategies alone are often insufficient to maintain triglycerides below the thresholds associated with pancreatitis risk. This underscores the need for continuous monitoring, family education, and multidisciplinary support. Looking ahead, emerging pharmacologic therapies targeting APO-CIII, ANGPTL3, and other pathways hold promise for patients with refractory or genetically determined hypertriglyceridemia. While their efficacy in adults is increasingly well documented, pediatric safety and effectiveness data remain scarce. Until such evidence becomes available, management in children must rely on a multimodal approach that combines rigorous dietary interventions with carefully selected pharmacologic agents when necessary. Collaborative research and pediatric-specific clinical trials are crucial to expand the therapeutic arsenal and improve long-term outcomes in this vulnerable population.

Endocrine Society will continue operating under a symposia time slot fee model for ENDO 2026. About ENDO ENDO is the signature annual meeting of the Endocrine Society and a highly sought-after international venue for highlighting the latest in endocrinology research and clinical care. In 2025, we welcomed top names in the fields of clinical endocrinology and hormone science research to deliver more than 185 educational sessions from leading experts from around the world including 75+ symposia sessions. ENDO 2025 also showcased 105 exhibiting companies, more than 2,700 new scientific abstracts, and 2510 scientific posters. chunks.content: Key Points Introduction Long regarded as a childhood disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is now recognised to persist across the lifespan [ ]. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition that has historically been underdiagnosed and undertreated in girls and women [ ], partly owing to subtler symptoms such as greater inattentiveness and internalising behaviours, compared with the more overtly hyperactive-impulsive presentation more common in men [ ]. Many women also adopt compensatory strategies, such as perfectionism, that can mask difficulties and further delay diagnosis [ , ]. Distinctive symptom expression may include excessive talking in childhood [ ], and in adult women, behaviours such as binge eating [ ], self-harm [ ] and emotional dysregulation [ ]. Comorbid conditions such as anxiety and depression may hide the underlying chronic persisting ADHD symptoms [ , ]. Apart from different symptom expression and comorbidities, women may also face unique challenges related to fluctuating hormones at different life stages: we recently highlighted these in a position paper on research advances and future directions in female ADHD [ ]. Hormonal Influences in the Menopausal Transition Perimenopause, the transition before menopause, is marked by hormonal changes and irregular menstrual periods. Oestrogen and progesterone levels fluctuate and progressively decline. Vasomotor symptoms such as hot flushes, night sweats and palpitations together with subjective cognitive complaints such as brain fog and memory complaints are especially common [ ]. Declining oestrogen levels also contribute to an increased risk of osteoporosis and cardiovascular disease particularly when menopause occurs early (before age 40 years) [ ]. Cardiovascular disease risk also rises post-menopause, as the protective effects of oestrogen on blood vessels and lipid metabolism diminish [ , ]. Other common symptoms include sleep disturbances [ ], musculoskeletal pain [ ] and genitourinary syndrome of menopause [ ], which reflects the broad impact of (peri)menopause on women’s physical health. Menopause may occur naturally (typical menopause) or be surgically induced following a bilateral oophorectomy, the latter causing an abrupt cessation of ovarian hormone production and typically a more severe symptomatic presentation. Symptom severity and duration during menopause vary widely. Symptoms can last a median of 4 years but may persist much longer in many [ ]. Symptoms are influenced by ethnicity [ ], psychosocial stress [ ], socioeconomic [ ] and lifestyle factors such as smoking [ ], alcohol use [ ] and physical activity [ ]. Menopause is defined as the moment following 12 months of amenorrhoea. The average age in the general population is 51 years [ ]. Hormones stabilise at very low levels in post-menopause. At this time, certain symptoms, like vaginal dryness and musculoskeletal pain, may persist or emerge [ ], while others (such as vasomotor symptoms and mood swings) may improve as hormone levels stabilise [ ]. Women with ADHD appear to have an earlier onset of natural menopause, an association reported in a genome-wide association study as well as in a population study from Iceland [ ]. While the background and implications of this association remain to be explored, earlier onset of natural menopause before age 45 years in general has been linked to a higher risk of all-cause mortality [ ]; cardiovascular disease [ ]; osteoporosis [ , ]; type 2 diabetes mellitus [ ]; Alzheimer’s disease and late-life memory decline [ , ]. In older adults with ADHD, susceptibility to cognitive impairment and dementia, particularly linked to white matter hyperintensities, is increased [ ]. Significant neuroendocrine fluctuations during the (peri)menopause and post-menopausal stages may exacerbate existing ADHD symptoms or unmask previously unrecognised cases. Several (peri)menopausal symptoms, such as forgetfulness, difficulty concentrating, mental confusion and executive dysfunction, overlap with those seen in ADHD [ ], complicating differential diagnosis. A recent population study in women aged 45–60 years showed that when ADHD symptom severity was assessed dimensionally, higher ADHD symptom levels correlated with more menopausal complaints (e.g. hot flushes, mood and memory issues [ ]). However, in the same study, a cross-sectional analysis found no significant differences in menopausal symptoms between women with and without a formal ADHD diagnosis. Nor were there interaction effects between ADHD diagnosis and menopausal stages (pre-, peri- or post-menopause) after correction for multiple comparisons. This suggests that symptom severity, rather than diagnosis presence alone, correlates with menopausal complaints [ ]. These hormonal fluctuations may also influence susceptibility and resilience to stress and cognitive-emotional processes relevant to ADHD, including attention, memory and emotional regulation, adding both diagnostic and therapeutic complexity [ , , ]. There is little known about the optimal pharmacological management of ADHD in (peri)menopausal women. In this narrative review, we synthesise the literature on the pharmacological management of ADHD across the (peri)menopause and post-menopause, focusing on the interplay between hormonal changes and symptomatology of ADHD. Based on our clinical experience and the (scarce) literature, we aim to provide practical guidance for

There is little known about the optimal pharmacological management of ADHD in (peri)menopausal women. In this narrative review, we synthesise the literature on the pharmacological management of ADHD across the (peri)menopause and post-menopause, focusing on the interplay between hormonal changes and symptomatology of ADHD. Based on our clinical experience and the (scarce) literature, we aim to provide practical guidance for pharmacological treatment of ADHD in this understudied population. Pathophysiology: Hormonal Interactions with Neurotransmitters Dopamine plays a central role in the pathophysiology of ADHD [ , ]. Dysregulated dopamine levels are associated with impaired attention and arousal functions [ ]. Extensive literature shows that oestrogen stimulates dopamine synthesis in the brain, reduces its reuptake and degradation [ – ], increases serotonin synthesis [ ] and modulates noradrenalinergic pathways [ ]. These actions are especially relevant in brain regions implicated in ADHD, such as the prefrontal cortex and basal ganglia [ ]. These areas are rich in oestrogen receptors and are critically involved in cognitive control and motivation. Stimulant medications commonly used in the pharmacology of ADHD may be more effective during high-oestrogen phases of the menstrual cycle and less effective when oestrogen is low, such as during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, postpartum, and during perimenopause, or menopause [ ]. Hormonal fluctuations may influence the efficacy of stimulant medications targeting the dopamine and noradrenaline systems, as reported by women during premenstrual and postpartum periods [ – ]. However, little is known about the effects of ADHD pharmacotherapy in postmenopausal women. The effect of progesterone on ADHD symptoms is complex. Overall, evidence suggests that it exerts an antagonistic effect on dopaminergic signalling. For example, preclinical studies have shown that progesterone, through its metabolite allopregnanolone, can inhibit dopamine release in the prefrontal cortex. By antagonising dopamine signalling and promoting sedation, progesterone may reduce stimulant efficacy and contribute to cognitive slowing and mood lability [ ]. Much remains unknown about ADHD during (peri)menopause. A systematic review found no empirical studies that investigated ADHD during menopause [ ]. However, the literature describing clinical experiences and non-peer reviewed preliminary findings suggest that many women report an exacerbation of ADHD symptoms during menopause [ , , ]. Our study of women with clinically diagnosed ADHD showed that they experience worse (peri)menopausal symptoms compared with women in the general population [ ]. Hence that low oestrogen environments are associated with increased ADHD symptom severity and possibly, reduced psychostimulant efficacy. Declining and erratic hormone levels during (peri)menopause may therefore worsen core ADHD symptoms, increase emotional dysregulation and diminish the effectiveness of usual pharmacotherapies. Pharmacokinetic and Pharmacodynamic Considerations During (Peri)Menopause Sex hormones modulate multiple pharmacokinetic pathways—affecting drug absorption, distribution, metabolism and clearance—as well as pharmacodynamic responses and adverse-effect profiles [ , ]. Women often show different drug responses to men, partly due to the interactions of oestrogen and progesterone with hepatic enzyme systems cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A4 and CYP2D6, which influence the metabolism of many centrally acting agents [ ]. During perimenopause, declining and fluctuating oestrogen levels can alter CYP activity (particularly CYP2D6 and CYP3A4) [ ], which may influence plasma concentrations of amphetamine and methylphenidate derivatives. Changes in body composition and reduced total body water may further affect drug distribution and peak concentrations [ , ]. Evidence from schizophrenia research suggests that oestrogen loss reduces the synthesis of enzymes that metabolise antipsychotic drugs, potentially weakening treatment efficacy [ ]. By analogy, similar mechanisms may contribute to reduced stimulant responsiveness in (peri)menopausal women with ADHD, although direct studies are lacking. To date, no studies have directly demonstrated pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic effects of reproductive-hormone fluctuations on psychostimulants, atomoxetine or bupropion. Available evidence is limited to indirect findings and theoretical mechanisms whereby oestrogen and progesterone may modulate hepatic CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 activity and catecholaminergic signalling [ , ]. Symptom Overlap and Diagnostic Challenges The symptomatic overlap between (peri)menopausal symptoms (e.g. brain fog, poor concentration, mood swings) and ADHD is substantial, requiring careful assessment. Emotional symptoms often intensify during (peri)menopause in women with ADHD, including increased anxiety, depression, mood lability and impulsivity [ , ]. Importantly, ADHD symptoms typically present from childhood and persist throughout life, whereas (peri)menopausal symptoms emerge later, around midlife. This is a useful distinction. Executive dysfunction during the menopause transition is influenced by both hormonal changes and psychological symptoms (anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance), which confound the assessment of cognitive symptoms in women with ADHD [ , ]. These findings emphasise how important a thorough clinical evaluation is to differentiate ADHD symptoms from cognitive changes related to (peri)menopause [ ]. Structured interviews for ADHD, such as the DIVA-5

Importantly, ADHD symptoms typically present from childhood and persist throughout life, whereas (peri)menopausal symptoms emerge later, around midlife. This is a useful distinction. Executive dysfunction during the menopause transition is influenced by both hormonal changes and psychological symptoms (anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance), which confound the assessment of cognitive symptoms in women with ADHD [ , ]. These findings emphasise how important a thorough clinical evaluation is to differentiate ADHD symptoms from cognitive changes related to (peri)menopause [ ]. Structured interviews for ADHD, such as the DIVA-5 (Diagnostic Interview for ADHD in Adults, version 5), are recommended, but should be administered and interpreted by clinicians familiar with both ADHD and (peri)menopausal symptomatology. All (peri)menopausal women with ADHD should be screened for psychiatric comorbidities such as anxiety, mood, sleep, substance abuse and personality disorders, which are common [ , ]. Executive dysfunction during the menopause transition varies by menopause type and is influenced by psychological symptoms, including anxiety, depression and sleep disturbance, which can obscure accurate assessment of cognitive difficulties [ ]. Cognitive and Attentional Changes During (Peri)Menopause: Overlap and Distinction from ADHD Although both ADHD and (peri)menopause can present with forgetfulness and concentration problems, their underlying mechanisms differ. In perimenopause, fluctuating oestrogen levels are associated primarily with inefficient attention and working-memory encoding, often perceived by patients as “memory loss”, whereas long-term storage and recognition remain intact [ , , ]. Consistent with this, in a large cross-sectional sample ( N = 1971), difficulties in executive function were significantly elevated in both (peri)menopausal and surgical postmenopausal women compared with premenopausal women [ ]. This finding supports the view that oestrogen decline contributes to deficits in executive control rather than true amnesia. By contrast, ADHD involves lifelong deficits in executive control and sustained attention. These deficits affect multiple cognitive domains, independent of hormonal status [ , ]. Sleep disturbance, vasomotor symptoms, and mood dysregulation during (peri)menopause further worsen attention, thereby increasing subjective cognitive complaints in women with and without ADHD [ , ]. Distinguishing between attentional inefficiency and true memory impairment is crucial for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning; targeted assessment of encoding, retrieval and executive functioning can help identify the dominant mechanism. When women present for a first-time ADHD evaluation during (peri)menopause, clinicians should take a detailed childhood symptom history, seek collateral information where possible and use a structured diagnostic interview such as the DIVA-5 to confirm persistence across the lifespan. As we recently outlined, clinicians can use structured history-taking and cycle-sensitive assessment protocols to distinguish hormonally mediated attentional inefficiency from underlying ADHD [ ]. In addition to pharmacological and hormonal approaches, non-pharmacological tools can further support symptom recognition and treatment optimisation. Regular use of mood- and cycle-tracking applications (e.g. Clue, Flo) enables women and clinicians to visualise fluctuations in attention, mood and medication response across hormonal phases. These digital tools facilitate shared decision making, track changes in cognition across the cycle, and can guide timing or dose adjustments of ADHD medication [ , ]. Such self-monitoring strategies are accessible, inexpensive and empower women to participate actively in the management of both (peri)menopausal and ADHD-related cognitive symptoms [ ]. Pharmacological Management of ADHD in Midlife Women Stimulant Medications Methylphenidate, dexamfetamine and lisdexamfetamine remain core psychostimulant pharmacotherapies for adult ADHD and have demonstrated efficacy in midlife [ ]. Lisdexamfetamine use in non-ADHD midlife women has been shown to improve executive function [ , , ]. Regarding methylphenidate, there are no randomised controlled trials specifically examining its efficacy in (peri)menopausal women with or without ADHD. This absence of trial data is noted in both an expert consensus statement on ADHD in women, which draws on clinical experience and broader adult ADHD research [ ], and a systematic review of ADHD and sex hormones in female individuals, which identified only indirect evidence from studies in younger women, small observational cohorts and hormonal phase comparisons [ ]. Similarly, for dexamfetamine, data from randomised controlled trials are lacking, although our case report study suggests dose responsiveness linked to premenstrual hormonal fluctuations [ ]. These findings highlight the need for further research on the effects of these medications specifically in women across the menopausal transition [ ]. Many women report that standard ADHD medications become less effective during (peri)menopause or require dose adjustments to offset hormone-related changes; however, formal scientific studies are lacking. Our small open study describing the effect of increasing psychostimulant dosage during the premenstrual period, with improved ADHD and mood symptoms, may indicate that hormone-related changes can necessitate dose adjustments [ ]. Guidelines suggest individualised treatment plans, which could be relevant for women experiencing hormonal changes during (peri)menopause [ ]. When using psychostimulants in midlife women, physicians should regularly monitor symptom control and side effects, effect on mood and sleep, as

transition [ ]. Many women report that standard ADHD medications become less effective during (peri)menopause or require dose adjustments to offset hormone-related changes; however, formal scientific studies are lacking. Our small open study describing the effect of increasing psychostimulant dosage during the premenstrual period, with improved ADHD and mood symptoms, may indicate that hormone-related changes can necessitate dose adjustments [ ]. Guidelines suggest individualised treatment plans, which could be relevant for women experiencing hormonal changes during (peri)menopause [ ]. When using psychostimulants in midlife women, physicians should regularly monitor symptom control and side effects, effect on mood and sleep, as well as blood pressure, pulse and weight. Cardiovascular risk rises with age and is further influenced by both ADHD itself and stimulant exposure [ ]. Genetic and epidemiologic studies demonstrate that ADHD itself confers an increased risk for cardiometabolic diseases (hypertension, obesity and cardiovascular disease) independent of medication use [ – ]. This may be due to underlying ADHD-related risk factors. Concerning the extra risk conferred using psychostimulants, in large cohort studies, a longer duration of ADHD medication use was modestly associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases (hypertension and arterial disease) [ ]. A meta-analysis found no consistent elevation in risk for major cardiovascular disease outcomes with ADHD medications, though a possible modest increase in cardiac arrhythmias was observed. The absolute incidence of these events remained very low (< 1% per year in adults), suggesting that while relative risks may increase slightly, the overall risk to most patients is small [ ]. A recent systematic review and randomised controlled trial analysis concluded that ADHD medications produce small increases in blood pressure and heart rate; nonetheless, the benefits of treatment generally outweigh these risks. The recommendation was careful cardiovascular monitoring during therapy [ ]. While much remains to be understood about the specific risk of cardiometabolic disease in (peri)menopausal women, it appears that women with ADHD have a significantly higher age-adjusted prevalence of cardiometabolic conditions [ ]. Our cardiology clinic study of mostly (peri)menopausal women with cardiovascular complaints found a high prevalence of lifetime ADHD symptoms using a screener [ ]. This may reflect the combined influence of hormonal changes and ADHD-related lifestyle and stress factors on increased cardiovascular risk. Non-stimulant Medications Atomoxetine has demonstrated benefit in a small study of (peri)menopausal women without ADHD [ ]. Guanfacine XR and Clonidine XR are alpha-2 agonists that may be considered for women who cannot tolerate stimulants or atomoxetine, although no specific evidence or guidelines address their use in (peri)menopausal women. Finally, bupropion may be helpful for comorbid depression and ADHD, but again, there is no evidence for benefits in (peri)menopause. If these medications are used, side effects should be monitored, especially blood pressure changes and sedation (in the case of alpha-2 agonists). Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors/serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors may be beneficial for women experiencing comorbid mood disorders [ ]; there is evidence that they also reduce the frequency and severity of hot flushes in (peri)menopausal and postmenopausal women [ , ]. Menopausal Hormone Therapy (MHT): Types and Timing Oestrogen therapy, particularly transdermal formulations (patches, gels) are recommended as they avoid venous thromboembolic and ischemic stroke events [ ]. They do not raise triglyceride levels [ ], and are considered safe regarding breast cancer risk [ , ]. Oestrogen is combined with oral micronised progesterone [ ], which has a better safety profile regarding breast tissue proliferation compared with synthetic progestogens [ ]. Clinical guidelines recognise that for symptomatic (peri)menopausal women aged under 60 years or within 10 years of menopause onset, the benefits of menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) generally outweigh the risks of breast cancer and cardiovascular disease [ , ]. These risks are lower than previously reported, based on updated analyses and re-evaluation of Women’s Health Initiative data, which support the ‘timing hypothesis’—that initiating MHT in women age under 60 years or within 10 years of menopause onset is associated with a more favourable benefit–risk profile [ , ]. Earlier initiation of MHT is most effective for cognitive and vasomotor symptom relief [ ]. Women should be screened for cardiovascular, thromboembolic and breast cancer risk before initiating MHT and the most appropriate therapy depending on risk/benefit considerations should be recommended [ ]. Potential Benefits for Cognitive, Sleep and Mood Symptoms Declining oestrogen during menopause has been implicated as a risk factor for cognitive decline, although consensus is still evolving [ ]. Experimental and clinical evidence indicates that oestradiol plays a role in modulating cognitive functions such as memory and attention through multiple neurobiological mechanisms, including genomic and rapid membrane receptor-mediated pathways [ ]. However, a systematic review and meta-analysis found that MHT had no overall effects on cognitive domain scores, including attention and working memory. Oestrogen therapy initiated close to menopause onset was associated with improved verbal memory [

recommended [ ]. Potential Benefits for Cognitive, Sleep and Mood Symptoms Declining oestrogen during menopause has been implicated as a risk factor for cognitive decline, although consensus is still evolving [ ]. Experimental and clinical evidence indicates that oestradiol plays a role in modulating cognitive functions such as memory and attention through multiple neurobiological mechanisms, including genomic and rapid membrane receptor-mediated pathways [ ]. However, a systematic review and meta-analysis found that MHT had no overall effects on cognitive domain scores, including attention and working memory. Oestrogen therapy initiated close to menopause onset was associated with improved verbal memory [ ]. Although targeted studies on sleep regulation in (peri)menopausal women with ADHD remain scarce, broader research clarifies the complex relationship between ADHD, hormonal changes and sleep. Sleep disorders are frequently observed in individuals with ADHD. Some evidence suggests that MHT stabilises the hormonal fluctuations underlying insomnia and circadian rhythm disturbances, which are prevalent during (peri)menopause [ , ]. Combining oestrogen with oral micronised progesterone can help alleviate vasomotor symptoms of (peri)menopause, such as hot flushes and night sweats, which often disrupt sleep, and progesterone may also help with falling asleep [ ]. Moreover, MHT protocols utilising micronised progesterone appear to present fewer side effects compared with those using synthetic progestogens such as dydrogesterone [ ]. Fluctuating hormone levels during menopause exacerbate sleep disturbances that can intensify ADHD-related cognitive and mood symptoms [ , ].Thus, by stabilising these fluctuations, MHT may indirectly alleviate not only sleep disruptions but also the associated cognitive and emotional challenges faced by women with ADHD. According to a systematic review of menopause guidelines, MHT, particularly oestrogen, is consistently recommended for (peri)menopausal mood disturbances, including low mood, which it improves [ , , ] and for mood changes [ ]. Women with ADHD have an increased risk for hormone-related mood disturbances [ ], and may therefore benefit from the positive effects of MHT on mood regulation. Cardiovascular and Bone Health Considerations Menopausal hormone therapy initiated early in the menopausal transition can slow the progression of atherosclerotic disease, lowering cardiovascular disease risk and mortality [ , ]. Meta‑analyses of randomised controlled trials demonstrate that MHT initiated in women aged younger than 60 years or within 10 years of menopause reduces all‑cause mortality by approximately 30–40% and coronary heart disease by roughly 30–50% [ ]. Additionally, it reduces osteoporosis risk by improving bone mineral density [ ].When initiated early in the perimenopausal period, oestrogen reduces fracture risk by 20–40% [ ]. Menopausal hormone therapy decreases bone resorption and enhances bone preservation, especially when combined with exercise [ ]. Sequencing ADHD Pharmacotherapy and MHT When a perimenopausal woman with ADHD is already taking an optimally titrated stimulant with minimal side effects but continues to experience perimenopausal symptoms, we add MHT where clinically indicated, rather than adjusting ADHD medication pre-emptively. Current evidence does not establish that stimulant doses routinely need modification in perimenopause. Therefore, ADHD pharmacotherapy should be maintained and monitored, with any subsequent dose changes guided by symptomatic response and tolerability over time [ , ]. Menopausal hormone therapy targets non-ADHD domains that may magnify cognitive and emotional difficulties (vasomotor symptoms, sleep, mood). Therefore, its initiation can indirectly improve daytime attention and executive functioning without necessarily altering stimulant requirements. When treatment changes are necessary, we prefer introducing one modification at a time, allowing clinicians to identify clearly which intervention produces benefit or side effects. Regular monitoring of cardiovascular status and sleep is recommended for both stimulant therapy and MHT. Clinical Guidance for Initiating and Adjusting Treatment In our clinical practice, prescription of MHT for (peri)menopausal women with ADHD is always individualised. We start with the lowest effective dose, in line with international guidelines, and only after excluding contraindications such as a history of venous thromboembolism, active or past breast cancer, uncontrolled hypertension or liver disease [ , , ]. For women with a uterus, systemic therapy always comprises oestradiol plus a progestogen to protect the endometrium [ ]. Our typical starting regime is the transdermal oestradiol patch 50 µg twice weekly plus daily micronised progesterone 100 mg at night [ ]. This approach reflects evidence that lower doses of both oestrogen and progesterone are sufficient for endometrial protection when combined appropriately [ ]. We monitor symptom response, bone health and risk profile, and titrate upwards only if necessary. Where patient preference or tolerability issues arise, we also offer other transdermal formulations (such as oestradiol gel or spray). All transdermal formulations confer a lower risk of venous thromboembolism compared with oral routes [ ]. Genitourinary syndrome of menopause may present with vaginal dryness, pain during sex and urinary urgency, including recurring urinary tract infections. In moderate-to-severe genitourinary symptoms, we add low-dose vaginal oestrogen, which improves urogenital health with minimal systemic absorption and risk [ , ]. This is also true in

Where patient preference or tolerability issues arise, we also offer other transdermal formulations (such as oestradiol gel or spray). All transdermal formulations confer a lower risk of venous thromboembolism compared with oral routes [ ]. Genitourinary syndrome of menopause may present with vaginal dryness, pain during sex and urinary urgency, including recurring urinary tract infections. In moderate-to-severe genitourinary symptoms, we add low-dose vaginal oestrogen, which improves urogenital health with minimal systemic absorption and risk [ , ]. This is also true in the case of previous breast cancer, where the decision to use vaginal oestrogen should be made in coordination with the treating oncologist. Current data do not show an increased risk of cancer recurrence for these women [ ]. Management should be multidisciplinary, involving clinicians with expertise in both menopausal care and adult ADHD. We refer to the general practitioner or gynaecologist for ongoing monitoring with an annual review of MHT (or earlier if needed). Symptom control and side effects are assessed. If relevant, bone density and breast health are assessed by the gynaecologist. In the Netherlands, we have a nationwide collaboration between general practitioners, psychiatrists, gynaecologists and cardiologists collaborating for integrated care for women with mental disorders facing hormonal fluctuations (H3: Head Heart Hormones network; https://www.h3-netwerk.nl/en/home-engels/ ). Concerning control of ADHD symptoms, we also dose individually, starting with the lowest effective dose of the stimulant, titrating as needed for symptom control and the side-effect profile. It remains unknown whether increasing stimulant or non-stimulant doses is beneficial when symptoms worsen during the (peri)menopause. This is an area requiring further research. Managing Comorbidities and Risk Factors Comorbidities should be addressed and if necessary, treated before commencing psychopharmacology for ADHD. Depression and anxiety disorders are common in both ADHD and (peri)menopause and may require additional pharmacotherapy (e.g. selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors). Sleep disorders should be identified and appropriately treated [ ]. Age-related sleep loss may be linked to lower melatonin production [ ]. A decrease in melatonin production has been described during (peri)menopause, with a steep decline post-menopause [ , ]. Melatonin has been reported to improve sleep and (peri)menopausal symptoms in several studies [ , ]. However, large-scale long-term trials are still needed to confirm its safety and sustained efficacy in (peri)menopausal women with ADHD. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder has been associated with inflammatory processes, as shown in studies of cytokine gene polymorphisms and cytokine levels in blood and cerebrospinal fluid, though findings are heterogeneous and sometimes contradictory [ ]. Neuroinflammation may contribute to ADHD via altered immune responses, genetic polymorphisms and prenatal inflammatory exposures, potentially affecting neurodevelopment and increasing ADHD risk [ ]. Evidence supports the beneficial effects of MHT on inflammation in (peri)menopausal women, particularly through modulation of cytokine levels and immune system interactions [ ]. However, this remains to be studied in (peri)menopausal women with ADHD. Given that both (peri)menopause and ADHD have been independently linked to inflammatory changes, it is plausible that their convergence could amplify neuroinflammatory processes, potentially influencing symptom severity and treatment response. Practical Screening Questions Before Initiating MHT in Women with ADHD Before initiating MHT, clinicians should systematically assess symptom patterns, risk factors and treatment goals; Table summarises key questions to guide this evaluation in perimenopausal women with ADHD. Future Directions and Research Gaps Despite growing clinical recognition of ADHD symptom exacerbation during the menopausal transition, empirical evidence to guide pharmacological management in this population remains limited. No randomised controlled trials have specifically evaluated stimulant or non-stimulant ADHD medications in (peri)menopausal or post-menopausal women, nor have studies examined optimal dose adjustment strategies during hormonal transitions. Current practice is informed largely by expert consensus, extrapolation from younger cohorts and small observational studies. Key research priorities include controlled trials assessing the efficacy and safety of ADHD pharmacotherapy across menopausal stages; investigation of potential interactions between stimulant medications and MHT; and longitudinal studies examining cardiovascular, cognitive and sleep outcomes in midlife women with ADHD. Improved understanding of these factors is essential to inform evidence-based individualised treatment approaches. Conclusions This narrative review highlights the unique challenges of pharmacological management of ADHD in women across (peri)menopause and post-menopause. Clinicians should be aware that women with ADHD entering this transitional phase may require careful re-evaluation of their pharmacotherapy. Symptom exacerbation is common because of declining and erratic oestrogen and progesterone, which may diminish medication effectiveness and worsen cognitive, mood or sleep disturbances. While MHT may offer benefits for vasomotor, mood and sleep symptoms, as well as cardiovascular and bone health, its impact on ADHD treatment outcomes has not been formally evaluated. Clinicians are encouraged to work with specialist colleagues in gynaecology and other relevant disciplines to optimise both ADHD and (peri)menopause management through individualised patient-centred care.

chunks.content: АКТУАЛЬНОСТЬ Врожденная дисфункция коры надпочечников (ВДКН) — это группа аутосомно-рецессивных заболеваний, характеризующихся дефектом одного из ферментов или транспортных белков, принимающих участие в синтезе кортизола в коре надпочечников [ ]. По последним данным, известно о 7 формах ВДКН, более 95% всех случаев связаны с дефицитом фермента 21-гидроксилазы [ ]. При данной форме наблюдается дефицит кортизола, что по принципу отрицательной обратной связи в оси гипоталамус-гипофиз-надпочечники приводит к повышению уровня адренокортикотропного гормона (АКТГ) и, как следствие, к гиперплазии надпочечников (рис. 1). В результате стимуляции надпочечников происходит избыточное накопление стероидов, предшествующих ферментативному блоку [ ][ ]. Распространенность классических форм дефицита 21-гидроксилазы составляет от 1:14 000 до 1:18 000 живых новорожденных в мире. По данным неонатального скрининга в РФ, распространенность заболевания в отдельных регионах составляет от 1:5000 до 1:12 000, в целом по стране — 1:9638 живых новорожденных. Неклассическая форма данного дефицита встречается чаще — от 1:500 до 1:1000 среди общей популяции, а в некоторых изолированных этнических группах, характеризующихся высоким процентом близкородственных браков (например, евреи Ашкенази), распространенность может доходить до 1:50 до 1:100 [ ][ ][ ]. Современные возможности скрининга новорожденных и вовремя начатая заместительная терапия глюкокортикостероидами (ГК) обеспечивают выживаемость детей с ВДКН. Неонатальный скрининг на 17-OH-прогестерон (17-ОНП) позволяет диагностировать классические формы дефицита 21-гидроксилазы. На втором этапе скрининга предпочтительно определение мультистероидного спектра методом тандемной масс-спектрометрии [ ]. Целью лечения ВДКН является восполнение дефицита кортизола путем назначения адекватных доз ГК, а при необходимости — и альдостерона, на фоне параллельной супрессии гиперсекреции АКТГ. Сложности в подборе адекватной дозы ГК с соблюдением баланса между неэффективным подавлением продукции АКТГ и ятрогенным гиперкортицизмом приводят к различного рода нарушениям, развивающимся с первых месяцев жизни и прогрессирующим с течением лет, часто приобретая особую клиническую значимость. При недостаточной дозе ГК может наблюдаться отсутствие адекватного подавления АКТГ, что приводит к гиперандрогении и росту образований в ткани надпочечников. Терапия, направленная на нормализацию АКТГ, зачастую приводит к передозировке ГК и связанным с ней рискам и осложнениям, таким как низкий конечный рост, ожирение, нарушение минеральной плотности костной ткани, бесплодие, сердечно-сосудистые заболевания, а также снижение качества жизни [ ][ ]. Патогенез метаболических нарушений при классических формах дефицита 21-гидроксилазы представлен на рисунке 2. В исследовании Arlt W. и соавт. у 203 пациентов с ВДКН была подтверждена высокая распространенность метаболических нарушений, таких как ожирение (с частотой 41% случаев), избыточная масса тела (37%), гиперхолестеринемия (46%), инсулинорезистентность (29%), остеопения (40%) и остеопороз (7%) [ ]. Схожие данные были получены и в российском исследовании 55 пациентов с классическими формами ВДКН в возрасте от 18 до 60 лет, в котором ИМТ≥25 кг/м2 встречался у 56% женщин и 47% мужчин, аналогично дислипидемия в 69 и 50%, артериальная гипертензия — в 10 и 14%, а нарушения углеводного обмена — в 17 и 7% случаев [ ]. Современное понимание проблемы ожирения встречается все чаще и чаще и говорит о том, что развитие тяжелых (морбидных) форм ожирения у пациентов с ВДКН связано не только с приемом высоких доз ГК, но и с нарушениями пищевого поведения и, таким образом, носит смешанный характер, в том числе и алиментарный. Сложный комбинированный генез сопутствующей коморбидной патологии у данной группы пациентов требует особых подходов в терапевтической стратегии, а отсутствие адекватного лечения приводит к декомпенсации основного заболевания, что требует увеличения доз ГК, образуя порочный круг. Таким образом, значимое снижение веса в комплексном лечении пациентов с ВДКН и ожирением играет одну из ведущих ролей. В настоящее время доказанно эффективным методом лечения ожирения, особенно морбидных форм, является бариатрическая хирургия. По ключевому механизму действия бариатрические вмешательства делят на преимущественно рестриктивные (рукавная резекция желудка) и преимущественно гипоабсорбтивные (одноанастомозное желудочное шунтирование, гастрошунтирование по Roux-en-Y и другие) [ ]. Бариатрическая хирургия не только приводит к значительному снижению веса, но и позволяет длительно удерживать достигнутые результаты под регулярным наблюдением и контролем эндокринолога, а также при выполнении послеоперационных рекомендаций. В доступной современной зарубежной литературе описан лишь единичный опыт выполнения бариатрической операции у пациентки с ВДКН. В 2017 г. группа исследователей из Клинического центра Национального института здоровья, Бетесда, Мэриленд, США во главе с Ashwini Mallappa опубликовала положительные результаты выполнения лапароскопической рукавной резекции пациентке с морбидным ожирением (МО) и ВДКН. Авторы отметили, что на фоне значительного снижения веса после операции удалось достигнуть снижения дозы принимаемых ГК, а именно доза гидрокортизона была снижена на 34% через 15 мес после операции [ ]. В отечественной литературе мы не встретили подобного опыта. Вашему вниманию представлен клинический случай успешного выполнения лапароскопической рукавной резекции желудка у пациентки с ВДКН и МО, ассоциированным с приемом ГК, а также нарушениями пищевого поведения.
